newsitem.title: GERMANY: German social partnership on line in sick pay row.
newsitem.headline: German social partnership on line in sick pay row.

text.p: Trade unions squared up on Sunday for a long battle over sick pay -- a conflict which could undermine the bedrock of Germany's social partnership.
Leading companies, headed by auto giant Daimler-Benz AG, have rushed to cut sick pay to the new legal minimum of 80 percent from October 1.
The unions, which struck for 16 weeks on the issue back in 1957 and won a 100 percent entitlement, are outraged.

At the centenary congress of the OeTV public workers union in Stuttgart on Sunday the mood was gloomy but defiant, and leaders seemed unlikely to heed calls for moderation from German President Roman Herzog.
Herzog, saying Germany must adapt to compete in a global market, called for employers and unions to cooperate "or else our social partnership cannot survive."
But OeTV chief Herbert Mai said that if his union gave ground on the sick pay issue it could be the first domino to fall in a series of benefit clauses locked into pay deals.
"Where we have contractual guarantees, employers will run into a brick wall," Mai told around 600 delegates.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl slashed minimum sick pay benefits by a fifth two weeks ago under a strategy to boost job creation and cut chronic absenteeism by workers entitled to six weeks of sick leave a year at full pay, on top of normal holidays.
Under Germany's system of industry-wide pay bargaining, application of such an entitlement cut would normally have been thrashed out at the negotiating table.
But Daimler broke ranks, incensing union leaders who say that the sick pay is written into their workers' contracts.
They called over 20,000 workers at three Mercedes plants to boycott extra weekend shifts, and OeTV delegates will protest at one factory on Tuesday in solidarity with workers there.
Hard-hitting Daimler chief executive Juergen Schrempp has defended the move, saying that the cuts in labour-related costs were needed to help defend German jobs and production.
"I call this credible, resolute action. We are fighting for Germany as a place to do business, for jobs and thus for its workers," Schrempp told the Focus news magazine.
Although big companies like Siemens AG have followed suit, others have been more cautious. BMW AG said it did not impose sick pay cuts "in the interests of internal company peace."
A survey of over 200 companies by Focus found that just 23 percent had decided to go ahead straight away with the cuts, while 63 percent would handle the matter in pay talks.

Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats, warned on Sunday that the abuse of wage contracts could lead to "major conflict", while the rush to implement the cuts has even dismayed some government leaders.
Rainer Eppelmann, social spokesman of Kohl's Christian Democrats, said employers were acting illegally.
"This is almost blackmail. I have the impression this is suicidal, if not kamikaze-like," Eppelmann told ZDF television.
German companies pay a whopping 60 billion marks in sick pay each year, and the country's workers are now ill more often than even Sweden's -- once Europe's "sickest" workforce.
But slashing the featherbed welfare state to get government finances into shape for European monetary union and reduce near record post-war unemployment will have a social price.

"The consensus between employers and workers, a pillar of the long-praised German model, collapsed long ago," news weekly Spiegel commented. "But within companies cooperation always worked well...That is over now."
